10. Comparability Over Time and Space

All the tide gauges included in this indicator have used the same methods for determining hourly water levels. These methods remained constant over time and across gauges, except as documented in NOAA (2014). Flooding thresholds have been established using the statistical model described in Sweet et al. (2018) that applies the same formula across all locations. Each location’s flood threshold has been applied consistently throughout the period of record, which supports this analysis of changes over time. NOAA’s scenarios have also been applied consistently over time and space.

The observed and projected time series cover the same spatial extent and resolution (the same set of tide gauge stations), and they apply the same indicator definition and thresholds.

11. Data Limitations

The technical documentation for the Coastal Flooding indicator identifies some factors that may impact the confidence, application, or conclusions that readers can draw from the observed portion of this pairing. For instance, the flood thresholds used for this indicator are derived from a statistical model, not directly based on local conditions, so they do not necessarily correspond to a consistent level of observed disruption or damage across different locations. Because coastal flooding relates to relative sea level (i.e., relative to the land surface elevation), projections must make assumptions about vertical land motion, which are based in part on historical observations.

12. Sources of Uncertainty

Observations inevitably reflect measurement uncertainty. Error measurements for each tide gauge station are described in NOAA (2009), although many of the estimates in that publication pertain to longer-term time series (i.e., the entire period of record at each station, not the exact period covered by the observed portion of this feature). Overall, tide gauges provide precise, reliable water level data for the locations where they are installed.

Interpreting projections requires users to consider scenario uncertainty. Projecting future conditions requires assumptions about future greenhouse gas emissions. This feature presents two widely used scenarios to illustrate a range of possibilities without assigning likelihoods to them, nor do these scenarios necessarily bound possible futures.

Sweet et al. (2022) discuss additional sources of uncertainty associated with projecting sea level rise and translating from global to regional estimates.

13. Sources of Variability

Changes in sea level and corresponding changes in coastal flooding can be influenced by multi-year cycles such as El Niño/La Niña and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation, which affect coastal ocean temperatures, salt content, winds, atmospheric pressure, and currents. The construction of this pairing addresses variability by presenting decadal averages.
